title: Effects of biophilic indoor environment on stress and anxiety recovery: A between-subjects experiment in virtual reality
research_question: Do biophilic indoor environments help people recover from stress and anxiety, and do these effects differ among different types of biophilic elements?

participants.description: Healthy adults (mean age 29.2 ± 11.8 years, 63% female, 41% white) affiliated with Harvard (faculty, staff, students).
participants.recruitment: Recruited via the Harvard Decision Science Lab (HDSL) recruitment system. Excluded participants who self-reported taking stress recovery medicine or therapy.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Four three-dimensional virtual offices simulated in VR (Rhino5, rendered in Unity): 1) Non-biophilic (control), 2) Indoor green (living walls, potted plants, water (fish tank), natural materials, biomorphic shapes), 3) Outdoor view (long-distance natural view of trees, grass, water, daylight through windows), 4) Combination (elements from both indoor green and outdoor view). All offices had the same size and similar layout.

mechanisms: Stress Reduction Theory (SRT): Exposure to nature activates the parasympathetic nervous system and facilitates psychophysiological stress recovery due to an innate preference for natural environments.
Attention Restoration Theory (ART): Natural environments with 'soft fascinations' replenish cognitive capacity, reduce mental fatigue, and increase focus and attention.
moderators: Type of biophilic element (indoor green, outdoor view, combination)
Recovery time course (immediate effects, larger impacts in the first four minutes of a 6-minute recovery process)
implementation_implications: Biophilic design elements can impact stress recovery and anxiety, providing evidence for architects, interior designers, and developers to select features that reduce stress and anxiety.
Virtual reality can be used to bring nature and its therapeutic benefits to patients in hospitals or individuals with reduced mobility.

tables.description: Characteristics of study participants (n = 100) and indoor environmental quality at baseline of the experiment.

limitations: VR simulations are not 'real world' conditions and do not include other sensory stimulations (auditory, olfactory, thermal comfort, people's interaction) that would be present in reality.
Did not measure changes in affective state of mood, which may mediate the pathway between biophilic environments and stress/anxiety.
Studies should be extended to indoor environments other than offices (e.g., assisted living, health care, hospitals, classroom, hospitality, retail).
